I have been thinking about how algorithmic social media feeds have changed my ability to focus. The problem is not that every post is bad or that I want to leave the internet. I still learn useful things, find thoughtful discussions, and keep up with friends. What bothers me is the rhythm the feed creates: a joke, a serious headline, a recipe, an argument, and a notification all arrive within the same minute. My attention keeps switching before it has time to settle anywhere.

I noticed the habit most clearly while reading. I would finish two pages, feel a tiny moment of uncertainty, and reach for my phone without making a conscious decision. There was rarely an important message waiting. The gesture itself had become a shortcut around boredom. Turning off nonessential notifications helped, but the stronger change was moving social apps away from the home screen and choosing two specific times to check them. @FocusFriend jokingly called this my “tiny waiting room for notifications,” and the name stuck. 📵

I do not think personal discipline is the whole answer. A feed designed to predict what will keep us scrolling has an advantage over a tired person at the end of the day. At the same time, blaming an algorithm for every distracted hour can become another way to avoid making choices. For me, the useful middle ground is to add friction: disable badges, keep the phone outside the room during demanding work, and follow people through deliberate lists instead of an endless recommended feed.

The surprising result is that social media feels better when I use less of it. I remember more of what I read, I reply with more care, and I no longer treat every quiet pause as a problem that needs content. I am not aiming for perfect concentration or a dramatic digital detox. I just want my attention to feel like something I direct, rather than something rented out in five-second pieces. #AttentionHabits
